results.question: What does the book say about making your own chroma keyer?
results.answer:
The book — *Digital Compositing for Film and Video*, Section 2.2 — describes two DIY approaches to building a chroma keyer, but it opens with a warning: unlike the luma keyer, where cleverness can meaningfully improve on the standard design, "making your own chroma keyer will probably be more hassle than it's worth," and an off-the-shelf chroma keyer "is hard to improve upon" [S3]. It still walks through the construction as an instructive exercise, "to test your mettle" [S3].

| Approach | Principle | How it's built | Book's verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Basic roll-your-own keyer (2.2.2) | Classic chroma key: convert RGB to HSV, key on color ranges | Start with an operation that converts RGB → HSV, pipe the HSV image into a color curve; RED curve = Hue, GREEN = Saturation, BLUE = Value (brightness), then adjust the three curves to include/exclude the target's ranges [S4] | More hassle than it's worth; harder to improve on than off-the-shelf [S3] |
| 3D color keyer (2.2.3) | Keys on any arbitrary color, not luminance — a "grossly simplified version" of Primatte's operating principles [S10] | Uses entirely different principles from the HSV approach; the book illustrates it by plotting green backing pixels in the RGB color cube (Figures 2.12–2.13) [S10] | Presented as an interesting, flexible variation [S10] |

The DIY build mirrors exactly how professional chroma keyers think: internally convert the RGB image to an HSV or HSL representation (RGB alone can't isolate saturation as a separate attribute), set a starting pixel as the "center" of the key, then define ranges for Hue, Saturation, and Value — pixels inside go to 100% white, outside to black, with adjustable tolerances on each range to soften the edges of the matte [S9]. That's the mechanism your home-built version is reproducing.

For practice, the book points to a test image, "Chroma key target.tif," designed for pulling chroma keys on various parts of the picture [S7]. One gap in the evidence: the book specifies no particular software or hardware requirements — the construction is described generically as an operation/node pipeline (RGB-to-HSV conversion feeding a color curve), the same style used for the luma keyer built in Section 2.1.3 [S4]. If you're looking for platform-specific instructions (Fusion, Nuke, After Effects), those aren't in the source material.

results.question: What does the book say about nonsquare pixels?
results.answer:
The core claim running across these sources is that a nonsquare pixel is a format convention, not a defect in the image data: its width and height are unequal, and the relationship is measured by the **pixel aspect ratio** (pixel width ÷ height) [S7][S8][S11]. On a properly adjusted computer monitor every pixel is the same width as its height — square pixels with a 1:1 ratio [S5]. The Art and Science of Digital Compositing adds a wry note that the shape is "rectangular rather than square" (actually oval rather than round, though "nobody ever uses the term 'nonround'") [S6].

**Where nonsquare pixels come from**

Nonsquare pixels appear when the aspect ratio of the displayed image differs from the aspect ratio of the original digital image, a situation that exists in both film and video formats [S6]. The classic example is standard-definition video: SD uses rectangular/nonsquare pixels (720×480 NTSC-DV, 720×576 PAL-DV), while HD, graphics-editing software, and computer monitors all use square pixels [S13]. Under the NTSC standard the pixel aspect ratio is 10:11 — pixels slightly taller than wide — so a digitally created perfect circle sent straight to an NTSC monitor displays as an ellipse stretched 11/10ths vertically unless you compensate [S17].

Film uses the same principle in a different name: because images sent to film no longer have identifiable pixels, the sources call those formats **squeezed** or **anamorphic** rather than nonsquare [S12]. Cinemascope, with its dramatic 2:1 squeeze, is the recurring example [S10].

| Context | Pixel shape | Pixel aspect ratio | Practical consequence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Computer monitors, HD, graphics software | Square | 1:1 | No correction needed [S5][S13] |
| SD video (NTSC) | Slightly taller than wide | 10:11 | Circles appear as ellipses without compensation [S17] |
| Anamorphic film (e.g., Cinemascope) | "Squeezed" (no physical pixels after film transfer) | ~2:1 in the example | Must unsqueeze before geometric operations [S10][S12] |

Two cautions run through the guidance. First, don't confuse pixel aspect ratio with the image's own aspect ratio — they are independent numbers [S11][S17]. Second, unsqueezing is only a display operation: the system applies a temporary geometric transformation so the image previews correctly, and the underlying image data is never modified [S9]. For compositing work, the author's standing advice is to unsqueeze an element before rotating it and resqueeze afterward — rotating a squeezed element directly produces visible distortion even at small angles (a 5° rotation still shows the error), so "double-check everything" when working with nonsquare pixels [S14]. You also need to know whether your software auto-compensates when sending images to video or whether you must scale manually [S17].

results.question: What does the book say about miscellaneous drawing tips?
results.answer:
The miscellaneous drawing tips in *Directing the Story* (Francis Glebas) appear across two sections with that heading, and they cluster around five practical themes: clarity, expressive posing, composition, anatomy, and a willingness to rework [S9][S12].

**Clarity and purpose**
- Draw for clarity — one idea per sketch, and draw attention to that one idea at a time [S9][S13].
- Have something to say in your image; don't doodle [S9].
- Highlight the important idea of the sketch and subordinate everything else to it [S12].
- Don't get too clever: tricky camera angles often just make the drawing ambiguous [S12].
- When drawing eyes, darken the pupils [S9].

**Expressive posing and feeling**
- Show how the character feels — feel the pose and the emotion in your own body as you draw [S12].
- A person is always "doing" something; express the purpose and experience the pose kinetically [S12].
- Use straight line symbols for stretches and bent line symbols for squashes [S12].
- Play straight lines against curves for interest [S9].
- Avoid symmetry — it is boring and makes drawings look cut out; use angles instead, since dynamic asymmetry is far more exciting [S12].
- Draw bold and expressive [S12].

**Composition and anatomy**
- Watch the body's landmarks where bones reach the surface, such as hipbones and ribs [S12].
- Draw borders so you have to compose to them [S12].

**Willingness to rework**
- Don't be afraid to redraw; keep searching for the best solution to tell the story [S9].
- If part of a drawing doesn't work, cut it out and rework it [S9].

Closely related advice appears elsewhere in the book: you should be able to blacken in your drawings and still read what's happening, keeping decoration inside the main outline so drawings don't get busy, with interesting outlines themselves [S8]. And mentor Vance Gerry's pragmatic rule: "If you can't photocopy it, trace it. If you can't trace it, then you'll have to draw it" [S14]. The cautions woven through all of it are consistent — avoid ambiguity, avoid decoration without meaning, and avoid symmetry — with the emphasis always on serving the story rather than cleverness.

results.question: What does the book say about transcoding versus color rerendering?
results.answer:
The VES Handbook draws a clear line between the two: **transcoding** is a numerical remapping of already-encoded colors between displays, while **color rerendering** is a perceptual re-interpretation that is only needed when the viewing environment itself changes.

**Transcoding** applies when the two displays' black levels, white luminance, viewing conditions, and gamma (signal-to-output) relationships are the same, and only the primary chromaticities differ [S4]. The procedure is purely arithmetic: linearize the first display's encoded RGB values, convert to CIE XYZ, convert those XYZ values to the second display's RGB, then reimpose the second display's encoding nonlinearity [S4].

**Color rerendering** becomes the right solution when contrast, white levels, or viewing conditions are grossly dissimilar [S3]. It works by undoing whatever color rendering was done — implicitly or explicitly — for the first display, then taking the resulting non-color-rendered CIE XYZ values and color rendering them anew for the second display [S3]. The Handbook defines color rendering itself as "the transformation of an image to account for differences in viewing environment" — the canonical example being a camera that color renders a JPEG captured in bright desert sunlight for reproduction on an office monitor whose peak white is hundreds of times dimmer, typically before quantization and rounding [S6].

The governing rule is that the complexity of the transform depends on the degree of difference between the two displays: small differences (different primaries only) degrade gracefully into transcoding; environment-level differences force a full rerender [S4].

| | Transcoding | Color rerendering |
|---|---|---|
| **Used when** | Black levels, white luminance, viewing conditions, gamma match; only primaries differ [S4] | Contrast, white levels, or viewing conditions are grossly dissimilar [S3] |
| **Operation** | Linearize → XYZ → second display's RGB → re-encode [S4] | Undo first display's color rendering → XYZ → color render for second display [S3] |
| **What changes** | Encoding numbers only | The perceptual appearance mapping itself |
| **Why** | The images are meant to be seen in the same way | The viewing environment makes the same numbers look wrong [S6] |

In practice this is why the decision is a judgment call, not a formula: as long as the displays represent the same intended viewing experience, a straightforward transcode preserves the image; once the destination environment meaningfully differs, numbers alone can't fix appearance, and a rerender is required.

results.question: What does the book say about affect, fatigue, and injury are control states?
results.answer:
Affect is the one member of your trio that the retrieved corpus genuinely treats as a control state, and it does so through two separate frameworks; fatigue and injury never appear as control states anywhere in the evidence, so those two premises are simply absent from the corpus. What follows covers the affect material in full, then names the missing pieces explicitly.

## Affect as a control state

**Dimensional affect models.** Russell’s circumplex organizes affect around valence (pleasantness–unpleasantness) and arousal (activation–deactivation), with each emotion understood as a combination of those two coordinates [S22, S26]. Mehrabian and Russell’s pleasure–arousal–dominance formulation adds a dominance dimension — control, power, or agency — and the Self-Assessment Manikin operationalizes all three through nonverbal rating scales [S22]. In the handbook’s CPCS glossary, **dominance/control** is defined as “perceived power, agency, or situational control in a VAD/PAD space,” permitted under the production alias VAC, and explicitly distinguished from model-guidance strength and from objective personality scores [S25]. The model is empirically grounded: factor analysis and multidimensional scaling repeatedly reproduce the two-dimensional structure across assessments, and arousal ratings track skin conductance and sympathetic nervous system activity [S34, S29].

**Laban Effort States.** The second framework treats affect as movement quality: two-factor combinations of the four Effort qualities — Weight, Space, Time, Flow — form six states, each a mood or “state of mind” that can motivate a character [S3, S31].

| State | Effort pair | What the sources add |
|---|---|---|
| Dream | Weight + Flow | the worked example of a State of Mind in the Laban Workbook [S3] |
| Awake | Time + Space | Dream’s opposite; practical, alert, sharpens thoughts and intuition [S3, S18] |
| Near (aka Rhythm) | Weight + Time | also called “rhythm state” [S3, S4, S31] |
| Remote | Space + Flow | also called “far state” [S3, S4] |
| Mobile | Time + Flow | combinations of flow and time effort [S14] |
| Stable | Weight + Space | steadfast attitude and physical presence; lacks the changeability of Time and the emotionality of Flow [S8] |

Each state has four possible “shades” or combinations — Stable offers direct/light, direct/strong, flexible/light, flexible/strong, while Awake offers direct or flexible × quick or sustained [S3, S8, S18]. The Workbook also maps states onto spatial planes: Stable to the Door plane, Near to the Wheel plane, Awake to the Table plane [S30].

**The control mechanism.** The key control lever is the gap between what a character feels and what they show. In the CPCS worked example “Dialogue Close-Up With Concealed Fear,” experienced affect moves from mildly negative to strongly negative, arousal spikes at the final word, and dominance drops then partially recovers — while displayed affect stays near neutral-positive, arousal rises only moderately, and dominance stays higher than experienced [S23, S28]. The corpus proposes a continuous affect vector A(t) = [valence, arousal, dominance], each coordinate in [–1, 1], as the usable cinematic control signal because it can vary smoothly across a shot; frightened-but-composed means negative valence, elevated arousal, moderate-to-high dominance, whereas panicked means low dominance [S21, S25]. Facial action units are the lower-level substrate: AU intensity is stored as a temporal curve, and an AU is explicitly not an emotion label [S25]. Work on Laban-guided generation reinforces the point — text prompts fail at controlling expressive detail, while continuous guidance-scale interpolation over Laban attributes yields fine-grained, relatively disentangled control [S32].

**Cinematic examples.** The evidence offers two film-level cases. Hitchcock’s sequence in *The Man Who Knew Too Much* builds its most tense moment from near-silence, with the isolation of McKenna underscored by muted, unorchestrated sound [S15]. In *Saving Private Ryan*, the sequence’s feeling state is mastery — Miller and his men read as experienced professionals, and the stretch carries the first note of hope within the larger 24-minute sequence [S11].

## Fatigue and injury: not covered

Neither **fatigue** nor **injury** appears anywhere in the retrieved material as a control state, with no definition, framework, or cinematic example for either. To answer those parts you would need a source the corpus does not supply — for instance, a Laban- or actor-training treatment of fatigue or injury as effort conditions, or a film-analysis account of them as expressive states. One disambiguation: the corpus does use “state” in a third sense — the carceral/surveillance state in *What the Face Reveals*, with fingerprinting, DNA swabs, and lifelong dossiers — but that material concerns state power over citizens, not control states in cinema [S1, S5, S13].

results.question: What does the book say about movement of an object with a background?
results.answer:
The book that addresses this most directly is Bruce Block's *The Visual Story*, which treats the background as the reference grid that makes object movement readable: an object moving against a background is never measured by itself, but by its changing position relative to the frame line and the stationary objects behind it [S24][S33].

**Definition.** Anything that moves in relation to the frame line is a moving object, and it generates a track — the path of its movement — categorized by direction, quality, scale, and speed [S26]. Against a background, two perception effects matter most. **Relative movement** occurs when an object's motion is gauged by its changing position against a second, stationary object — e.g., a circle that appears to move because it shifts relative to a fixed green circle and the frame [S24][S33]. **Induced movement** occurs when a moving object transfers its motion to a nearby stationary object, so the background seems to move while the actual mover appears still [S22]. The strongest possible contrast is no movement at all — tableau staging, where the stationary arrangement of objects carries the scene [S23] — and movement can even continue across cuts, with shot #2 starting where shot #1's track ended [S28].

**Case study.** The book's key example is a car driving a circle around a camera in a forest while the camera pans to keep up: the car stays in the same place relative to the frame, so there is no relative movement, yet the background trees sweep through the frame and generate apparent movement, which the viewer transfers onto the car [S34].

```
camera pans to follow the car
car stays fixed against the frame
trees sweep past in the opposite direction
→ viewer reads "the car is moving"
```

**Cinematic techniques.** The same principle drives the craft advice in the other sources. Tracking alongside a character or vehicle emphasizes the moving background and the sweep of motion [S35]; shooting through or past foreground objects introduces motion parallax, which conveys the position and distance of players and objects in the scene [S30]; and circling a static subject on a telephoto lens makes the background appear to revolve so quickly it can visualize a character's psychological breakdown — the apparent background speed grows with the subject-to-background distance, the camera's circling speed, and focal length [S29]. In compositing, the background is literally engineered to match the motion: match moving extracts tracking data from the foreground image so the background moves correctly when the camera moves [S27], and tracked background plates can be attached to follow the camera move of the foreground shot [S25].

results.question: What does the book say about sound editing?
results.answer:
The corpus's editing texts treat sound editing as a creative foundation rather than a cleanup job: it is "even more elaborate and requires many more decisions than the picture edit," because a wrong decision can undermine the visuals [S18]. What production failed to record is created in postproduction, and the editor's first task is to determine the scene's **narrative point** and surround it with sound [S18][S28].

**What it involves**

A film's sound design is an aural universe built from layers of dialogue, sound effects, music, ambient sounds (atmospheres), and sometimes voice-over [S24]. The sound designer oversees the overall acoustic experience and its many tracks — dialogue, ambience, hard sound effects, and foley — while the sound effects editor places each effect into its corresponding track [S23][S25]. Track counts run from roughly 6–16 for simple films up to 60 in a feature, and the same care in building and mixing applies to everything from a two-track music video to a 62-track blockbuster [S24][S30][S21].

**Key principles**

- **Believability first.** Because sound is processed faster than visuals, believability is magnified as a problem: if the sound isn't believable, the visuals are undermined and audience involvement is lost. Narrative clarity and believability are the primary goals of the sound edit [S28].
- **Emotional power.** Auditory stimuli affect humans on physiological, psychological, and emotional levels; "silent" films were never intended to be silent — only technology kept them mute [S22].
- **Storytelling over realism.** Almost everything that matters on screen should have sound, even if it would be silent in real life — fight sound effects are explicitly about storytelling, not reality [S14].
- **Sound builds worlds.** In a scene from the corpus's example, the adolescent world is defined by exciting music while the adult world is quiet, almost despairing natural sound — the sound design leads in creating that contrast [S7].

**Process and techniques**

During the rough cut, only the tracks needed for dramatic decisions are edited (dialogue and scratch music). After picture lock, the multi-track sound design is built one track at a time, then equalized and mixed down to a master — stereo at the simplest, 5.1 surround for cinema [S24]. Creative sound work begins once the dialogue edit is finished [S23]. The mix itself is where separation and linkage happen: keeping effects on separate tracks lets the mixer fade one out and another up for smooth transitions, while a continuing sound carried over two disparate visuals implies a link between shots, the passage of time, or continuity [S30]. Historically, this sophistication took time to arrive — when sync dialogue first appeared, cutting meant losing sound and image, so editing was restricted to silent sequences until rerecording and multiple cameras became common [S31].

One note: the Walter Murch material in this corpus is his career biography (Oscars, mixing and editing credits, restoration work) rather than a theory of sound editing [S1][S4][S5][S8]. The substantive points above come from the editing and directing manuals — Dancyger, *Grammar of the Edit*, the DaVinci Resolve guide, and Rabiger & Hurbis-Cherrier.

results.question: What does the book say about write radio sparely?
results.answer:
**Hey Whipple, Squeeze This** makes "write sparely" the default rule for radio copy. Unless the concept genuinely demands a lot of words and fast action, keep the script lean — spare writing is what lets voice talent read slowly, quietly, one word at a time [S8]. And the instruction holds even when the idea isn't a bare-bones one: a fat script at the studio means editing under pressure, without client approval [S9].

The book gives two structural reasons to stay lean. Most radio spots are promotional in nature, and clients add promotional tags at the end, which eats into total time, so "remember, write sparely" [S7]. A :30 is an even more extreme case — "maybe 60 words" — closer in discipline to a 10-second TV spot, where comedy has to hit fast, "a quick pie in the face" [S10]. The payoff is what the book calls "the remarkable power in silence": silence is to radio what white space is to print, and it enlarges the idea it surrounds [S19].

Its own model is a premise that rolls out in seconds: an announcer on the street gathering consumer reaction to the leading brand of dog food, answered only by voices shouting "Yelllllchh! Aaaarrrrrgh! Gross! This tastes awful!" [S10].
